summary: Market sentiment turned notably risk-off as optimism over a potential US-Iran nuclear deal collapsed, with Iran's security council declaring the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed unless Washington meets its conditions, sending Wall Street and Gulf equity markets lower in tandem. The dominant macro driver is escalating Middle East geopolitical tension, with Iran threatening continued closure of the Hormuz Strait — through which roughly 20% of global oil supply transits — while Trump openly stated options include letting Iran "fail economically" or striking the country militarily. Oil prices continued to climb on supply disruption fears, while on the equity side Cardinal Health surged after issuing strong profit guidance, Nvidia received a positive catalyst from its financing push per Cramer, and rotation was evident as one institutional portfolio exited an industrial position to add an AI play and initiated a stake in a memory chipmaker. The primary risk factors investors are monitoring include a full Hormuz blockade disrupting global energy flows, expanding Red Sea conflict after multiple Houthi attacks killed crew members and a US vessel fired on a ship attempting to break an Iranian port blockade, and potential inflationary spillover from sustained oil price gains. In the short term, markets are likely to remain volatile and headline-driven, with any diplomatic breakthrough on Iran capable of triggering a sharp relief rally, while further escalation — particularly involving the Strait of Hormuz — could push oil materially higher and pressure equity valuations, especially in energy-import-sensitive sectors.
